{{Infobox U.S. congressional committee|name={{PAGENAME}}|type=standing|chamber=house|congress=118th|image=Edworkforce2.png|image_size=250|caption=Committee logo|formed=March 21, 1867|former_names={{bulleted list |Committee on Education and Labor|Committee on Education|Committee on Labor|Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities}}|chair=[[Virginia Foxx]]|ranking_member=[[Bobby Scott (politician)|Bobby Scott]]|rm_party=D|rm_since=January 3, 2023|chair_party=R|chair_since=January 3, 2023|seats= 45 members|majority1=R|majority1_seats=25|minority1=D|minority1_seats=20|website=https://edworkforce.house.gov/|senate_counterpart=[[United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions]]}}{{United States House of Representatives}}
The '''Committee on Education and the Workforce''' is a [[Standing committee (United States Congress)|standing committee]] of the [[United States House of Representatives]]. There are 45 members of this committee. Since 2023, the chair of the Education and the Workforce committee is [[Virginia Foxx]] of [[North Carolina]].

==History of the committee==
Attempts were made to create a congressional committee on education and labor starting with the early congresses but issues over Congress's constitutional ability to oversee such issues delayed the committee's formation. Finally, on March 21, 1867, the '''Committee on Education and Labor''' was founded following the end of the [[American Civil War|Civil War]] and during the rapid industrialization of America. On December 19, 1883, the committee was divided into two, the '''Committee on Education''' and the '''Committee on Labor'''. The committees again merged on January 2, 1947, after the passage of the [[Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946]], becoming the Committee on Education and Labor again.  

=== Name changes ===
On January 4, 1995, when the Republicans took over the House, the committee was renamed the '''Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities'''. It was renamed again as the '''Committee on Education and the Workforce''' two years later on January 7, 1997. On January 4, 2007, with the Democrats once again in the majority, the committee's name was changed back to Committee on Education and Labor.<ref>[https://www.archives.gov/legislative/guide/house/chapter-09.html Chapter 9. Records of the Committees on Education and Labor], ''Guide to the Records of the U.S. House of Representatives at the National Archives, 1789-1989'' (Record Group 233), [[National Archives and Records Administration]]</ref> After Republicans recaptured the House majority in the 2010 elections, they returned to the name, Committee on Education and the Workforce, effective with the opening of the [[112th Congress]] in 2011.<ref>[https://blogs.wsj.com/washwire/2010/12/24/republicans-labor-to-avoid-labor/ Wall Street Journal: Republicans Labor to Avoid ‘Labor’]</ref> After Democrats recaptured the House majority in the 2018 elections, they similarly returned to the previous name, Committee on Education and Labor, effective with the opening of the [[116th Congress]] in 2019.{{cn|date=September 2022}} 
With the passing of the new House Rules associated to the Speaker negotiations in January of 2023, the 118th Congress renamed the committee as the Committee on Education and the Workforce again.<ref>[https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/there-are-new-house-rules-under-gop-leadership-heres-a-short-guide PBS: There are new House rules under GOP leadership. Here’s a short guide]</ref>

== Activity ==
In December 2023, the Committee held a [[2023 United States Congress hearing on antisemitism|hearing on antisemitism]] at which three university presidents were invited to speak about their handling of antisemitism on their campuses, and later pressured to resign.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Borter |first=Gabriella |last2=Morgan |first2=David |date=December 8, 2023 |title=U.S. lawmakers demand Harvard, MIT, Penn remove presidents after antisemitism hearing |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/wharton-letter-adds-pressure-penn-president-resign-2023-12-08/ |publisher=Reuters}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-02 |title=New York Post: Harvard President Claudine Gay's resignation 'just the beginning of reckoning' amid House antisemitism probe: Stefanik |url=https://stefanik.house.gov/2024/1/icymi-new-york-post-harvard-president-claudine-gay-s-resignation-just-the-beginning-of-reckoning-amid-house-antisemitism-probe-stefanik |access-date=2024-01-11 |website=Congresswoman Elise Stefanik |language=en}}</ref> Ultimately, within weeks the [[List of presidents of the University of Pennsylvania|president of the University of Pennsylvania]], [[M. Elizabeth Magill]], resigned as direct consequence of the hearing, and Claudine Gay, [[president of Harvard University]] was forced out because of plagiarism accusations amplified in part due to the hearing.

An April 2024 hearing with [[President of Columbia University|Columbia University president]] [[Minouche Shafik]] was held later in the morning of the first day of the [[2024 Columbia University pro-Palestinian campus occupation]]. Shafik resigned as President on August 14th of that same year.
